summary: The timeline's own bar now carries a zoom, so a recording longer than a few seconds can be worked on a second at a time instead of as a sliver. Open it out around the playhead, see where you are in the whole recording on a thin bar over the ruler, and press Fit to get the whole thing back.
setup: Photonz Dev, Experiments window, release Next. Open a recording (or the sample one) so the timeline is up. The flag is next-open-out-the-timeline and it is on by default in Next; next-sound-on-the-timeline gives the waveform this is best judged on.

try.do: Open a recording and cut it into a few pieces with B, so there are joins to aim at.
Look at the right hand end of the TIMELINE bar: a minus, a plus, what is on screen said as two moments, and Fit.
Press the plus three times and watch the playhead: it stays on the same pixel while the ruler shrinks to half a minute.
Press the plus until the ruler counts in tenths of a second, then put a cut on a particular sound in the waveform.
Drag the thin bar over the ruler to move along the recording, and press somewhere else on it to jump there.
Pinch on the lanes with two fingers to open out around the point under them.
Press space and watch a zoomed timeline play: the window pages along with the playhead.
Press Fit to put the whole recording back across the width in one go.

evaluate: Is doubling the right size of step, or does getting from the whole recording to one second of it feel like too many presses?
When you press the plus, does the timeline open out where you expected, or does it move something you were looking at?
Does the thin bar over the ruler tell you where you are quickly enough, or do you find yourself pressing Fit just to get your bearings?
Is 1:00 to 1:30 the right thing for the readout to say, or would you rather it said how far in you are?
Playing a zoomed timeline jumps a screenful at a time rather than scrolling smoothly. Does that read as keeping up, or as jumping?
rough: There is no keyboard shortcut. Every other timeline in the world zooms on plus and minus, and those keys are left alone here because the canvas already has a zoom and a key that means two zooms is worse than one you have to reach for.

The two finger pinch is the one part of this a walk cannot drive, so it is built and compiled and has not been watched working. Everything else in this list was driven by the walk that ships with it (open-out-the-timeline-walk), which left seven real pictures of the window.

The only way to move along a zoomed timeline with the pointer is the bar over the ruler. Two fingers sideways over the lanes does nothing, because the lanes already scroll up and down and SwiftUI hands a view no sideways scroll without dropping to AppKit.
The readout rounds to whole seconds, so at the closest window it can say 4:56 to 4:58 while the ruler above it is counting tenths. It is never wrong, but it is coarser than what it is describing.
How far you have opened the timeline out is forgotten when the window closes. Coming back to a recording puts the playhead where you left it and the timeline at the whole thing.
A picked piece is drawn in solid accent, which makes its waveform hard to read at exactly the zoom where the waveform became worth reading.

The walk stands in for a five minute recording by sliding the eight second sample to the five minute mark: a document's duration follows what is in it, so empty time cannot be faked, and there is no long recording in the repo to test on.
